claims.text: The onset of yielding in single-crystal FeNiCrMn is controlled by thermally activated dislocation nucleation at solute-induced lattice-friction barriers.
Yielding is not primarily controlled by stress-driven dislocation nucleation.
Local lattice distortion arising from differences between constituent atoms impedes dislocation motion and produces strengthening.
Chemical short-range order or local lattice distortion raises the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation.
The FeNiCrMn alloy initially forms an FCC solid solution.
The initial FeNiCrMn single crystal is free of precipitates and secondary phases.
The anomalous strain-rate insensitivity of yield strength results from the solute-friction-controlled mechanism.
At low temperatures, thermal activation over high lattice-distortion barriers controls yield.
Thermal activation over high barriers makes yield less sensitive to strain rate.
Diffusion-assisted deformation mechanisms can become active at higher temperatures.
Deformation twinning acts as a secondary plasticity carrier.
FCC-to-HCP transformation acts as a secondary plasticity carrier.
Twinning and FCC-to-HCP transformation are orientation dependent.
Yield strength will depend only weakly, logarithmically, or sub-linearly on strain rate, especially at cryogenic temperatures.
Dislocation glide, twinning, and FCC-to-HCP transformation will be the dominant deformation modes.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation will occur during the elastic-to-plastic transition.
Crystal orientation significantly changes yield stress through anisotropic resolved shear stress on slip and twinning systems.
Traditional FCC metals such as Ag and Cu are highly strain-rate sensitive because they have lower lattice friction and lack multicomponent solute drag.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to polycrystals when grain-boundary sliding or BCC precipitation dominates.
Stress-induced phase transformation remains possible in HEAs with reduced solid-solution phase stability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis labels twinning and FCC-to-HCP transformation as secondary carriers, whereas the predicted outcome includes twinning and FCC-to-HCP transformation among the dominant deformation modes.

The mechanism attributes weak rate sensitivity to thermal activation, while the falsification rule contrasts that behavior with a strong linear rate dependence described as characteristic of athermal glide; the proposed rate-dependence distinction is not internally explained or quantitatively defined.
